sentences: A single face fills a sheet of paper not much bigger than two open hands, just 38.
5 by 20.5 centimetres.
There are no visible ears, no neck, no body: only eyes staring straight ahead and a beard that flares out like a flame.
The painter is Yun Du-seo, a late Joseon scholar-painter known as Gongjae.
He was the great-grandson of the poet Yun Seon-do and the maternal great-grandfather of Jeong Yak-yong.
After a brother died in political exile, he gave up office for scholarship and painting.
The black cap at the top is a tanggeon, worn by officials beneath their wide-brimmed hats.
Here its top is cut off by the edge of the paper.
That pushes the face right up toward us, making it feel even more overwhelming.
Now meet his eyes, locked straight onto yours.
They seem to look right through us.
Critics praise how the pupils, added as a final touch, bring the whole face to life and capture the sitter's very spirit.
Rather than clean outlines, the face is built from countless tiny brushstrokes.
Where the strokes gather, the skin darkens, revealing every contour.
The raised brows and full lips speak of a firm, unbending character.
Look closely at the side whiskers and beard.
Each hair is drawn one fine stroke at a time, so the beard bursts outward like a flame.
His friend Yi Ha-gon is said to have written a poem about his long beard blowing in the wind.
For years some scholars thought this portrait was unfinished.
Then in 2006 the National Museum of Korea examined it with infrared and X-ray imaging, and found that both ears had once been painted on either side of the face.
In the empty space below, the collar and folds of a robe were found as well.
A 1937 photograph in a colonial-era survey still showed the collar.
Over nearly three hundred years the lighter lines and colours simply faded away, and fade is the right word: only the face remained.
The study also revealed colour applied to the back of the paper so that it glows softly through to the front.
Some scholars, however, find the revealed ears oddly shaped and suspect they may be a later addition.
Joseon portraits usually showed sitters at a slight angle in formal official robes, so a bare, head-on self-portrait like this one was radical in its own time.
Today it is a National Treasure, kept at Nogudang, the family seat in Haenam.
Yun is said to have painted this face while studying his own reflection in a mirror.
Step back one last time and meet his gaze again.
What question was this scholar asking himself in that mirror, three hundred years ago?
